transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Hi. Yeah, it’s nice to meet you too. Well, the main reason I’m here... it’s mostly because of what's been happening at my job. I work as a cashier, just down at the grocery store. I actually have a bachelor's degree, but, well, the cashier job is what pays the bills right now, and it’s usually fine. But lately, things have been going wrong right at the register. 

I just keep getting... I guess you'd call it stuck? I get stuck doing these things that absolutely do not fit the moment. Like, I’ll be scanning a box of cereal or a carton of milk, and suddenly I’m just tapping the scanner. Just tapping it in this very specific pattern, over and over, and I just keep doing it while the customer is standing right there staring at me. Or, even worse, the transaction goes through and the cash drawer pops open, and I’ll reach in to grab a five-dollar bill or some quarters, and my hand just stops. It completely freezes right over the money. I’ll just be standing there like a statue with my hand hovering over the cash drawer, and the customer is waiting for their change, and the line is backing up all the way down the aisle, and people are sighing and shifting from foot to foot... and I just can't seem to move my arm to finish handing them their money. 

It’s been happening a lot, and it's causing a real problem because last week my manager pulled me into the back office and he actually wrote me up for it. He handed me this official written warning because he said I was holding up the lines and acting strange. So since my job is on the line now, I figured I really had to come in and talk to someone about why I keep freezing up like that.
When you start tapping the scanner in that pattern, does it feel like you have to do it to relieve a strong urge or anxiety?

No, it really isn't like that at all. I know exactly what you mean by anxiety, like that tight, heavy feeling you get in your chest when you're worried about paying the electric bill, or when you see the store manager walking down your aisle with his little clipboard. But it is absolutely not that. I don't have any sort of thought in my head that if I don't tap the scanner, something terrible is going to happen. There is no buildup of tension beforehand, and there is certainly no sense of relief when I do it. 

It’s just... well, I’ll be scanning, right? I've got the barcode lined up on the red laser, maybe it's a can of soup. A lot of people buy the chunky soups, usually the clam chowder or the beef stew, especially since it was just on sale for two for four dollars last Tuesday. And my hand just starts doing the tapping. Tap, tap, tap. Just like that. It’s almost like my arm just decides to execute this physical motion entirely on its own, completely disconnected from my brain or whatever I’m actually focusing on at that exact second. 

Because if it was driven by anxiety, I think I would feel nervous beforehand, wouldn't I? But I am not nervous in the slightest until after I realize I am stuck doing it and the customer is just glaring at me. Like this one older lady, she comes in every Thursday morning right after we open, always buys the exact same brand of cat food, the little fancy foil tins. And I was tapping the scanner against her tin of salmon paté, and she looked at me with her eyes wide open, just completely bewildered. Now, that is when I got anxious, seeing her face. But before that? During the actual tapping? No, there is no urge whatsoever. It just happens. And I really can't explain why it happens, which honestly is the most infuriating part of this entire ordeal. Because you see, if it was just regular anxiety, maybe I could just take a deep breath and force myself to stop, but I just keep tapping regardless of how I feel.
When the tapping starts, can you stop it if you try?

Well, that's the thing, isn't it? That's exactly the crux of the whole issue. When it starts... I try. I really do try. I’ll be standing there, looking at my hand doing this tap-tap-tapping motion against the scanner, or I'll be frozen like a statue with my hand hovering right over the fives and tens in the till, and my brain is screaming at me to just move. Just stop tapping, just grab the money, just finish the transaction so this person can take their groceries and leave. 

But I can't. I just... I get completely stuck. Like I told you earlier, that's the whole reason I'm sitting here in this chair right now. I keep getting stuck doing these bizarre things that absolutely do not fit the moment, right there at the register. The tapping, the freezing with my hand over the open cash drawer while the customer is standing there sighing and checking their watch... I can't just snap out of it. If I could stop it, I wouldn't have gotten written up by my manager last week. I would have just stopped tapping the scanner and handed the lady her change, and everything would have been fine. But my body just won't listen to me when it happens. It just keeps going, or it stays frozen, no matter how hard I try to force myself to just act normal.
Since childhood, have social situations usually been hard for you to understand?

Social situations? Oh, no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, growing up, I was always pretty good at reading people, you know? Like back in grade school, I remember this one time in the fourth grade, we had this teacher, Mrs. Gable, and she was always very strict about where we sat during lunch. But I could always tell exactly when she was in a good mood, usually on Fridays when they served those little square pizzas, and I knew just how to ask her if I could sit with my friends instead of at my assigned table. I was always very attuned to that sort of thing. 

Even now, at the grocery store, before all this tapping and freezing business started, I was great with the customers. I know how to make small talk, how to read their body language. You can always tell when someone is in a rush because they'll start aggressively shifting their weight, or they'll have their credit card pinched between their fingers before I've even finished scanning their first item. And I know how to adjust, how to just give them a quick nod and speed up the scanning. Or if it's someone who wants to chat, like that older lady with the cat food I mentioned, I know exactly how to listen and smile. So, no, understanding social situations has never been a problem for me. It's just this physical stuff, this getting stuck, that's completely out of left field and ruining everything. I've always been perfectly fine with the social side of things, completely normal in that regard.
Have you been hearing voices when no one is there?

Voices? Well, yes, actually. I wasn't sure if I should even bring that up, but since you're asking... yes. Most days, actually. It's the strangest thing, and it really throws me off my rhythm at work. I'll be standing there at my lane, and I hear what sounds exactly like a couple of people talking, just right off to the side of me. Not far away, but like they are standing just a few feet over my shoulder. 

Sometimes, especially if I'm stationed at Register 6, which is the one right by the big gray swinging doors that lead into the back, I'll hear them calling my name from the stockroom. Clear as a bell. I'll hear my name being called out, and I'll actually crane my neck to look, thinking maybe the shift supervisor needs me to do a price check or grab a fresh roll of receipt paper. But the doors aren't moving. There's nobody there. 

And then other times, and this is the part that really makes me second-guess myself, I'll be right in the middle of a transaction. I could be ringing up produce—say, the green bell peppers, which you have to weigh and key in manually, PLU 4065, I know them all by heart—and right as I'm typing it in, I hear these voices saying I rang something up wrong. They'll just be talking to each other, saying, "He messed that up," or "He charged them for the wrong item." And it sounds so real, so incredibly distinct, that I immediately stop and spin around to see who is standing behind my lane critiquing my work. Because nobody likes a backseat driver, right? Especially when I have a bachelor's degree and I know exactly what I'm doing with these codes. 

But every single time I turn around... nothing. Just empty space, or the magazine rack, or the endcap with the half-price seasonal candy. There is absolutely nobody there. And I'll ask the customer, or I'll ask Brenda in the next lane over, "Did you just hear someone say that? Did you hear someone talking?" And they always just stare at me and shake their heads. No one else ever hears it. But I swear to you, it sounds as real as you talking to me right now, and it is incredibly distracting when you're trying
When your hand starts tapping or freezes, does it feel like some outside force is controlling your body?

An outside force? Controlling me? No, no, it’s nothing like that. I mean, I know it sounds completely bizarre, what with the tapping and the freezing up and the voices I was just telling you about, but I’ve never once felt like someone or something else was pulling my strings, like a puppet or something. It’s not like there’s some invisible hand reaching down and forcing my fingers to tap against the scanner, or some alien beam locking my muscles in place over the cash drawer. 

It’s just... it’s me. It’s my hand, my arm, my body. It’s just that my body isn't listening to my brain. It’s more like a misfire, you know? Like when you try to start a car and the engine just cranks and cranks but won't turn over, no matter how hard you turn the key. The key is turning, the signal is being sent, but the machinery just isn't cooperating. I’m the one turning the key. I’m the one screaming in my head, "Move your hand! Stop tapping! Give the lady her change!" But the transmission is just shot. 

So, no, I don't feel possessed or controlled by anything outside of myself. I’m fully aware that it’s my own body betraying me. Which, honestly, is almost more frustrating, because if it was an outside force, at least I could blame that, right? I could say, "Hey, it wasn't me, it was the invisible force!" But it is me. It’s just me, standing there at Register 6, looking like a complete fool while my hand does its own little tap dance or turns to stone, and I can't do a single thing to override it. It’s a total breakdown in communication between my brain and my arm, but it’s all happening inside my own system. No outside interference at all.
Do the voices ever comment on what you are doing as you do it?

Well, yes, actually, they do. I think I mentioned that a moment ago, but it's really the most prominent part of it. They absolutely comment on what I'm doing, right in the moment. Like I was saying about the produce—the green bell peppers, or the Honeycrisp apples, which are PLU 3283, by the way. I'll be right in the middle of typing the code, my fingers actually on the keypad, and I'll hear them. Just these two voices, talking to each other, not even to me directly, but about me. 

They'll say things like, "He messed that up," or "He charged them for the wrong item." And it's so immediate, right as I'm doing the action. It's not like a memory or an echo from earlier in the day; it's a live commentary, like a sports announcer calling a game, but it's just two people standing right over my shoulder critiquing my scanning technique. And I'll stop—I mean, you would too, right? If someone was standing behind you at your job telling you you were doing it wrong? I stop, I turn around, fully expecting to see a manager or a customer who got too close, but there's just the magazine rack. The People magazine, the TV Guide, but no actual people. And I'll ask Brenda, who's been at the store for fifteen years, "Did you hear that?" And she just looks at me like I've sprouted a second head. So, yes, they comment exactly as I'm doing things, and it is incredibly disruptive when you're just trying to get through a line of customers.
When your hand freezes in place, does it stay in that exact position for a while even if it would be awkward or uncomfortable?

Oh, absolutely. Yes, it stays right there. It’s... well, honestly, it’s actually the whole reason I finally decided I needed to come in and see someone. Because it doesn't just freeze for a split second and then I recover. I just keep getting stuck doing these things that completely don’t fit the moment, and it lasts long enough to cause a real scene. 

Like I was saying before about the tapping—tapping the scanner in this specific pattern—or, to answer your question, freezing with my hand right over the open cash drawer. The drawer pops open, I reach out to grab the bills, and my hand just stops in mid-air. And it stays there, suspended. You know, cash registers are positioned a bit low, so you have to lean forward slightly, which is not a natural posture to hold. So my shoulder will start to ache, and my lower back gets stiff, and it is physically very uncomfortable to just hover your arm like that. But I can't pull it back and I can't move it forward. 

And the social awkwardness of it is just agonizing. The customer is just standing there waiting, right? They’re staring at me, usually holding their hand out for their change, maybe sighing or shifting their weight, and I'm just frozen like a statue over the twenty-dollar bills. I can see them looking at me like I've lost my mind, but I just can't complete the motion to hand them their money. 

It’s incredibly embarrassing, and to be perfectly frank, it's threatening my job now. Last week, it got me written up. I had this woman buying a huge cart of groceries—lots of canned goods, mostly soup, which takes forever to bag anyway—and when it came time to give her change, I froze. I was stuck for so long that she actually leaned over the counter and yelled for a manager. My shift supervisor, Gary, had to come over and physically close my till, and then he pulled me into the back office by the breakroom. He gave me a formal written warning. He actually wrote down that I was "intentionally delaying service" and exhibiting bizarre behavior on the floor. Intentionally! As if I wanted to stand there with my arm cramping up while a woman yelled at me over a few dollars in change. So, yes, when it freezes, it stays exactly in that position, no matter how much it hurts or how inappropriate it is for the situation.
If someone gently moves your frozen arm into a new position while you're stuck, does it stay in that new position?

Well, it’s funny you ask that specific question, because... yes. Yes, it does. And I know I literally just told you about this, about how the whole reason I came in is because at the register I keep getting stuck doing things that completely don’t fit the moment, but that’s exactly what happened during that incident I just mentioned. 

When I was freezing with my hand over the cash drawer while the customer was waiting—the woman with all the soup, remember?—when Gary finally stomped over, he was furious. He didn't just reach around me to close the till. He actually grabbed my forearm to push my hand out of the way so he could slam the drawer shut. He didn't hit me or anything, he just firmly pushed my arm down and to the left to clear the space. 

And... I just stayed like that. My arm just stayed exactly
Do you believe anyone is trying to harm you or spy on you?

No, no, I don't think so. I mean, nobody is actively trying to hurt me, or following me around with cameras or anything like that. I know some people get like that, where they think the government is tapping their phones or their neighbors are plotting against them, but I don't have any of those thoughts. It's really just the voices at work, and the freezing up, and the... the physical things. 

Like Gary, my supervisor—he was mad, sure, but he wasn't trying to harm me when he moved my arm. He was just frustrated because the line was backing up past the frozen foods aisle, and he had to deal with the customer who was complaining. He’s just a guy trying to run a grocery store, you know? He’s not out to get me. And Brenda, the other cashier I mentioned, she’s actually very sweet. She brought me a piece of banana bread she baked last week. So, no, I don't feel threatened by anyone. I don't feel like I'm in danger or being watched, outside of just the normal feeling of being watched by customers when you're ringing them up, which is just part of the job. It's a very public-facing job, being a cashier, so you're always sort of on display, but not in a sinister way. Not like spying. Just... people waiting for their groceries. So, no, nothing like that.
Have you noticed yourself speaking much less than usual lately?

Well, yes, actually. I have. And my wife has definitely noticed it, too. It’s... it’s hard to explain, because it’s not like I’m giving people the silent treatment or anything like that. I still care about her, and I still care about my kids, obviously. Very much so. But lately, when people ask me questions, or even just try to make normal conversation, I just... I don't know, I mostly just shrug. I just can't seem to find much to say. 

It’s like the well is just dry. For example, my son is away at college right now—he’s in his sophomore year, studying engineering, which is incredibly demanding—and usually, I’d be calling him every Sunday evening. We had this whole routine where we’d talk about his classes, and I’d give him advice on his car because it’s an older model and always needs something tweaked. But lately... I just don't have the push to pick up the phone. The drive to do it is just gone. My wife will say, "Aren't you going to call him?" and I just kind of look at her and shrug. I want to, in theory, but the actual effort of speaking, of coming up with the words and keeping a conversation going, it just feels like climbing a mountain.

And it’s not just talking, it’s... it’s everything. I used to be very active. I have this kayak group that meets up on Saturday mornings down by the river. We’ve been doing it for years. We get out there early, paddle for a few hours, and then usually grab coffee afterward. But I haven't gone in weeks. I just can't muster the energy or the interest to get the kayak down from the garage rafters, strap it to the car, and go. Even my little repair projects around the house—I love tinkering, fixing radios, rewiring old lamps, that sort of thing. I have a whole workbench set up in the basement with all my tools organized on a pegboard. But I haven't touched any of it. I just sit there. And when my wife asks what's wrong, or why I'm so quiet, I just... I don't have an answer for her. I just shrug. Because I really don't know what to say. The words just aren't there anymore.
When someone tells you to make a simple movement during one of these stuck episodes, do you automatically do exactly what they say?

Well, if they just *tell* me to do something? I'm... I'm really not sure. I don't know if I automatically follow verbal instructions like that when I'm in the middle of it. Like I said before with Gary, he physically grabbed my arm and moved it, and my arm just stayed there. But if someone just said, "Hey, move your hand," I don't know if my body would listen or if I'd just stay frozen. 

Because, like I was saying earlier—and I know I keep bringing it back to the grocery store, but that really is the whole reason I came in to see you in the first place—I just keep getting stuck doing these things that completely don't fit the moment. I know I already mentioned freezing with my hand over the cash drawer while that customer was waiting, but it's not just the freezing. It's other things, too. 

Like, last week, I got stuck tapping the scanner. You know the barcode scanner? The big flat glass one built into the counter where you also weigh the produce? I was just standing there, tapping the glass in this very specific pattern with my knuckles. Just tap, tap, pause, tap... over and over. It made absolutely no sense for the situation. The customer was just staring at me, waiting for me to scan her items, and I knew she was waiting, but I was just stuck doing that pattern. 

And that's actually what finally did it. That incident last week is what got me written up. Gary pulled me into the back office—it’s this tiny little room right next to the employee break area, barely enough space for a desk and a filing cabinet—and he handed me a formal written warning. When someone moves one of your limbs during one of these frozen episodes, does it stay in the new position?

Well, yes, actually. That’s exactly what happened with Gary, like I was trying to explain. When I’m stuck, and someone physically moves my arm or my leg, it just... stays there. It stays right where they put it, like I’m a mannequin or a clay figure or something. 

When Gary grabbed my arm that day at the register—he grabbed me right by the forearm, just above the wrist—and he pulled my hand away from the cash drawer because I had just been hovering there, completely frozen, while the customer was getting more and more agitated. He moved my arm down toward my side, and when he let go, my arm just stayed there, hovering in mid-air, slightly bent at the elbow. It didn't drop back down naturally like it should have. It just held that exact position he left it in, and I didn't even try to move it back. I couldn't. 

And, you know, it’s not just the freezing up, either, which is what I was trying to say before. I keep getting stuck doing these things that completely don't fit the moment at all. Like the tapping. I mentioned the tapping, right? On the glass scanner? I was just standing there, tapping this very specific pattern with my knuckles on the glass where you weigh the apples and the potatoes. Tap, tap, pause, tap. Over and over again. The customer was just staring at me, waiting for me to scan her groceries—she had a whole cart full, mostly canned goods and some frozen dinners—and I knew she was waiting, but I was just stuck doing that pattern. 

And that’s the whole reason I came in to see you. Because it’s affecting my job. That tapping incident last week? That’s what finally got me written up. Gary pulled me into the back office—the one by the break room with the old coffee machine that always smells like burnt plastic—and he gave me a formal written warning. I have a bachelor’s degree, you know? I shouldn't be getting written up at a grocery store for tapping on a scanner, but I just... I get stuck. Whether it’s freezing with my hand over the drawer or tapping the glass, I just get stuck, and if someone moves me, I just stay right where they put me.
During these episodes, do you ever find yourself repeating another person's words exactly after they speak?

Repeating their words? No, no, I don't think I do that. If a customer asks if we have any more of the sale paper towels in the back, I don't say it back to them. I mean, I might not say anything at all, like I was telling you earlier about just shrugging when the well runs dry, but I definitely don't echo people. It's not my words that get stuck on a loop, it's... well, it's my actions. 

I know I'm sounding like a broken record here, Doctor, and I know we just went over this, but it really is the entire reason I'm sitting in this chair right now. I just keep getting stuck doing these physical things at the register that completely don't fit the moment. Like I was saying with the tapping on the scanner glass in that weird pattern, or when I just froze with my hand hovering right over the open cash drawer while that lady was standing there waiting for her change. It makes absolutely no sense for the situation, but my body just does it anyway. 

And it's humiliating, frankly. I'm fifty-four years old, I have a bachelor's degree, and yet last week I got a formal written warning because of it. Gary pulling me into that tiny back office to write me up like I'm some teenager goofing off on my first job... that's what finally made me come in to see you. I just can't keep getting stuck doing these bizarre things when I'm supposed to be ringing people up.
Have other people told you that your face looks blank or that you show much less emotion than usual?

Well, my wife has said something like that, yeah. She says I look... flat. Like I'm just not reacting to things the way I used to. And it's not that I don't care! I want to make that very clear, Doctor. I still care deeply about my wife, and my kids. My son is off at college right now—he's a sophomore, studying engineering, doing really well—and I love him to pieces, but... I just don't seem to have the push to call him. It's like the energy it takes to pick up the phone and dial the number and have a conversation is just completely gone. 

And it's not just calling him. It's everything. I used to meet up with this kayak group on the weekends down by the river. We'd go out for hours, paddle around, grab a burger afterward. But lately, I just... I can't bring myself to go. The drive, getting the kayak off the roof rack, the whole social aspect of it... it just feels like climbing a mountain. Even my little repair projects around the house. I used to love tinkering with things in the garage—fixing old radios, rewiring lamps, that sort of thing. I have a whole workbench set up with all my tools perfectly organized. But now, I just walk past it. I look at it, and I just don't have the drive to even pick up a screwdriver. 

And when my wife or my friends ask me what's wrong, or why I'm not coming out with the kayak group, or why I haven't called my son... I don't even know how to explain it to them. I mostly just shrug. I just shrug because I can't find much to say. The well just runs dry, like I was telling you earlier. It's like the words and the energy and the... the spark, I guess, is just missing. So yeah, I guess my face probably does look blank, because that's exactly how I feel inside. Just... blank.
Outside of work, have you ever suddenly held a strange posture and stayed that way for a long time?

Outside of work? You mean like at the house, or when I'm out running errands? Honestly, no, I haven't really noticed myself holding any strange postures at home. Or, I mean, maybe I do and there's just no one around to point it out, since my wife works during the day and my son is off at college. But really, I don't think so. 

I know you're trying to ask about other parts of my life, Doctor, and I know I'm probably beating a dead horse here, but I just have to stress that the store is where this is really destroying me. It’s exactly like I was trying to explain earlier. I came in to see you specifically because at the register, I just keep getting stuck doing these things that completely don’t fit the moment. It's not happening when I'm sitting on my couch watching TV, it's happening when I'm supposed to be working. 

Like that time I just froze completely with my hand hovering right over the open cash drawer. I was just stuck in that posture, hovering there like a statue, while the customer was standing there staring at me, waiting for her change. It makes absolutely no sense to do that. Or the tapping thing I mentioned, where I get stuck tapping the glass scanner in that specific pattern when I should be scanning groceries. The customer is just waiting, and I'm just... stuck. 

And that’s the whole crux of it, really. If this was just happening in my garage, maybe I wouldn't be sitting here right now. But it’s happening at the register, in front of customers, and it’s affecting my job. That's why I'm here. Because last week, it finally got me written up. Gary gave me that formal warning, and it just... it really shook me. I'm fifty-four years old, I have a bachelor's degree, and I'm getting disciplined because my body just decides to freeze or tap on things instead of doing my job. So, outside of work, I don't think so. But at work... it's a disaster.
Have these freezing or unusual postures ever happened anywhere other than at the grocery store?

I... well, I know you're trying to get a sense of the bigger picture here, Doctor, trying to see if this is happening everywhere, but I really have to be honest with you. It's the store. It's always at the store. I mean, I was just saying this, but it really is the whole reason I'm here. I came in because at the register, I just keep getting stuck doing these things that completely don't fit the moment. 

It's not like I'm standing in line at the post office and suddenly freeze up, or I'm at the gas station and start tapping on the pump. It's when I'm behind my own register. Like I told you, I'll just freeze completely with my hand hovering right over the open cash drawer. I'll have the bills right there, the customer is standing across from me, looking at me, waiting for their change, and my hand is just stuck in mid-air. Or the tapping... I'll just start tapping the glass scanner in this specific pattern, over and over, when I should be scanning a box of cereal or a bag of apples. 

And I know I keep bringing this up, but it's because it's so incredibly stressful. It's not just a little quirk, it's affecting my livelihood. Last week, it got me written up. Gary pulled me into that tiny, cramped back office—the one that always smells a little bit like stale coffee and floor wax—and he handed me a formal written warning. Me. A fifty-four-year-old man with a bachelor's degree, getting a disciplinary write-up because my body decides to just... short-circuit while I'm trying to ring up groceries. So, no, I haven't noticed it happening anywhere else. It's the store. It's always at the store, and it's ruining everything.
When you use your hands for other tasks at home, like buttoning a shirt, do they ever freeze or get stuck?

Buttoning a shirt? No, no, nothing like that. I wake up, I put on my uniform—it's this standard blue polo with the company logo they make us wear—and I button it right up, no problem at all. I tie my shoes, I pour my coffee from the pot... my hands work perfectly fine for all of those normal, everyday things. 

I... look, Doctor, I feel like we're going in circles here, and I really don't mean to be difficult. I know you have a checklist of things you have to ask, but I feel like I'm just repeating myself because you're looking for a problem where there isn't one. The problem isn't at home with my clothes. The problem is exactly what I've been trying to get across this whole time. I came in to see you specifically because at the register, I just keep getting stuck doing these things that completely don’t fit the moment. 

It's not my shirt buttons, it's the cash drawer! Like I was saying before, I'll just freeze completely with my hand hovering right over the open till, the bills right there at my fingertips, while the customer is just standing there staring at me, waiting for their change. Or I'll get caught up doing that tapping thing, tapping the scanner in that specific pattern instead of actually scanning the groceries. It only happens there, when I'm on the clock, and it's serious. It's incredibly serious to me. Like I told you, last week it got me written up by my manager. A formal disciplinary warning in my file. That's the crisis here, Doctor. That's what I need help with, not my buttons.
If something suddenly distracts you during one of these episodes at the register, does your hand start moving normally again?

Well, that's the thing, isn't it? Distractions. A grocery store is nothing but distractions. You've got the intercom blaring about a spill in aisle four, you've got kids screaming because their mom won't buy them a candy bar, you've got the beep-beep-beep of the other registers... it's a sensory nightmare on the best of days. But when I'm stuck? When I'm in the middle of one of these... whatever they are... it's like all of that noise just fades out. 

So, if a customer clears their throat loudly, or if the bagger asks me a question, does it snap me out of it? No. Not really. I might hear them, somewhere in the distance, but my body just won't listen. It's exactly what I've been trying to tell you, Doctor. I came in because at the register, I just keep getting stuck doing these things that completely don't fit the moment. 

It's not like a daydream where you snap out of it when someone snaps their fingers. When I freeze with my hand over the cash drawer, it's like my arm turns to lead. The customer is waiting, maybe they're sighing or shifting their weight, and I'm just hovering there. Or the tapping... I'll be tapping that scanner in my pattern, and someone could drop a whole jar of pickles right next to me, and I'd probably just keep tapping until the urge or the... the glitch... finally passes.
